items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Nursing Values: Students’ Perceptions of Trust, Empathy, and Future Roles
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in healthcare systems, creating new opportunities to enhance efficiency, optimize workflows, and strengthen patient monitoring. At the same time, its integration raises important questions about ethics, trust, and the preservation of humanistic values in nursing practice.Aim: To investigate nursing students’ awareness, attitudes, trust, and visions regarding the integration of AI in healthcare and nursing practice.Methods: A descriptive cross‑sectional design was applied, involving 140 nursing students. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire that explored awareness, attitudes, trust, and expectations regarding AI in healthcare. The analysis combined descriptive statistics with inferential techniques, including correlation and regression, to identify relationships among the variables.Results: Seventy‑two percent of participants had heard of AI in medicine, but knowledge levels were moderate (M = 3.3). While 43% believed AI could support nurses and 66% saw potential for improved patient care, 60% expressed discomfort with AI‑led care. Empathy and human contact were rated as highly important (M = 3.6 and M = 3.7 respectively), and 83% rejected full replacement of nurses. Trust was limited, with only 32% believing AI reduces medical errors. A majority (57%) envisioned a human‑centered future, with AI serving as a supportive tool rather than a substitute.Conclusion: Nursing students recognize the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) but remain cautious, emphasizing humanistic values and expressing skepticism about safety and trust. They envision a human‑centered future where AI supports nursing practice without replacing its essential human role, highlighting the need for balanced integration through education, policy, and further research.

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence applications in surgical pathology encompass tumour detection, histological classification, grading, biomarker assessment, lymph node evaluation, margin analysis, and outcome prediction. Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high diagnostic performance across multiple malignancies including breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, and gastrointestinal cancers. Emerging computational pathology platforms can predict molecular alterations directly from routine haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, facilitating personalized treatment strategies while reducing dependence on expensive ancillary testing. AI-assisted pathology has also improved workflow efficiency, reduced interobserver variability, and enhanced diagnostic reproducibility. Importantly, AI-derived pathological insights are increasingly influencing surgical decision-making through improved risk stratification, optimized extent of resection, tailored lymphadenectomy, and prediction of treatment response.

items.abstract: BackgroundThis study investigates the complex relationship between perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) opportunities and well-being, exploring the underlying psychological processes. Using conservation of resources theory, we examine how employees who view AI as an opportunity report better workplace well-being and show greater adaptive thinking capacity. Conversely, perceptions of unemployment risk appear to be linked to challenges in cognitive reappraisal, which, in turn, correlate with diminished well-being.ObjectiveTo assess the relationships among these constructs, including the specific relationship between employment insecurity and well-being, to understand how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress.MethodsThis research, conducted among 201 professionals in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, uses convenience sampling and structural equation modeling (analyzed using SPSS and SmartPLS) to assess relationships among these constructs, including the relationship between employment insecurity and well-being.ResultsThe findings suggest that optimism and hope about AI may support psychological resilience, whereas concerns about displacement are negatively correlated with employee well-being.ConclusionUltimately, while grounded in a specific context, this study offers wider implications, showing how AI is experienced as both a valuable tool and a source of stress, depending largely on an individual's assessment of the related risks in their professional environment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for full-cycle clinical management in orthokeratology: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: The global myopia epidemic, especially among children, poses a major public health burden. Orthokeratology (OK) is an established intervention for slowing myopia progression, yet its conventional practice is constrained by variable treatment responses, an experience-dependent fitting process, and the need for vigilant long-term safety monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an approach to enhance precision, efficiency, and accessibility across the entire OK care cycle. This review assesses AI applications in OK, encompassing pre-treatment efficacy prediction, AI-assisted lens fitting and automated fit assessment during treatment, and post-treatment safety monitoring with complication risk alert. Evidence indicates that AI models perform comparably to, and in some tasks surpass, human experts in predicting outcomes and determining optimal lens parameters. However, translation from research to routine practice is hindered by limited data quality and diversity, the opacity of complex algorithms, insufficient external validation, and unresolved ethical concerns. Progress depends on building large-scale, diverse datasets, developing interpretable and robust models, and fostering effective human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Imbalanced Financial Classification and Its Societal Implications for Digital Trust: A Cost-Sensitive XGBoost–Transformer Ensemble
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates how financial institutions decide who is trusted, who is scrutinised, and who is refused — decisions that carry direct social consequences for individuals and communities. Automated credit-risk and fraud-assessment systems are deployed at a scale where their errors are not merely statistical but socially consequential, because they can restrict access to credit, widen financial exclusion, and erode public confidence in digital finance. This paper addresses one technical precondition for trustworthy deployment: reliable learning from severely imbalanced financial data. It treats the task as what the data actually measure — prediction of credit-card default rather than verified fraud — and proposes FraudShield, a hybrid framework that combines a gradient-boosting model (XGBoost), a Transformer-based tabular model, an adaptive gating mechanism that learns a per-instance weighting of the two branches, and a cost-sensitive decision layer that reflects the unequal social and economic cost of different errors. The framework is evaluated on the UCI Credit Card Default dataset (30,000 clients), whose positive (default) class comprises 22.12% of the observations — a ratio of approximately 1:3.52. The evaluation protocol splits the data before any preprocessing, fits target encoding and standardization within each training fold only, and applies SMOTE to the training folds alone. Under this corrected protocol, FraudShield attains an AUC-ROC of 0.943 and an F1-score of 0.892, and the cost-sensitive layer raises measured cost savings from 16.7% to 28.4% over the majority-class baseline. The paper interprets these results within a broader discussion of AI accountability, fairness, and digital trust, and argues that technically sound imbalanced-learning methods are a necessary — though not sufficient — condition for socially responsible automated decision-making in finance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Work: Ethics, Responsibility, and Practical Applications
items.abstract: Workshop held at the Leipzig University Library (more info here). Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research, but how can we use these technologies responsibly? This workshop goes beyond simply presenting AI tools and instead focuses on the ethical, legal, and sustainable aspects of their application. We critically discuss how AI systems can influence scientific integrity, from data quality to potential biases in research results. Central to this are good scientific practice, data protection, copyright, and sustainability: How can researchers trustfully integrate AI tools without compromising reproducibility or ethical standards? We also explore ethical challenges such as transparency, fairness, and the long-term consequences of AI usage. Only after clarifying these core questions we address practical use: Which AI tools are suitable for which research goals? The workshop provides an insight into the opportunities and risks of AI in science, with the goal of equipping participants with a clear understanding of essential safeguards and best practices, as well as a practical, secure workflow to confidently integrate AI tools into their research without compromising scientific integrity, reproducibility, or compliance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Surrogacy: Legal Challenges, Liability, and the Protection of Vulnerable Parties
items.abstract: Despite the promise of better outcomes and efficiency, artificial intelligence in reproductive technology is changing the legal environment for surrogacy and complicating the family law landscape. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to match intended parents with surrogate mothers, conduct medical screenings and assist parents in making decisions. While the development is bringing benefits, the uncertainty created is uncontrolled. This paper examines the legal implications of AI-assisted surrogacy, focusing on issues of liability, contractual validity, and the determination of parental rights. The involvement of algorithmic systems challenges traditional legal principles, particularly in situations where harm may result from automated decisions or inaccurate data. The lack of transparency further complicates the allocation of responsibility among the different actors involved. From a human rights perspective, the use of AI in surrogacy raises concerns regarding the protection of the best interests of the child, as well as the autonomy and dignity of surrogate mothers. The paper highlights the risks of exploitation and unequal power relations, which may be intensified through technological mediation, especially in cross-border contexts. The paper argues that current legal frameworks are not adequately equipped to regulate the intersection between artificial intelligence and surrogacy, emphasizing the need for clearer legal standards and stronger regulatory oversight to ensure the protection of vulnerable parties.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Whistleblowing Systems, and Professional Skepticism in Higher-Education Fraud Detection
items.abstract: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of digital media engagement and user sentiment using machine learning techniques
items.abstract: Abstract Digital media datasets consist of both text content and platform, campaign, temporal, and engagement data, but precomputed sentiment and engagement data can lead to target leakage and overestimation of model performance. This study introduces the Hybrid Textual Sentiment Engagement Learning Model (HTSELM), a leakage-controlled late-fusion model for sentiment and engagement analysis. The experiments are conducted with the machine-generated Social Media Engagement Dataset, which has 28 raw columns and 12,000 records. Deterministic Affective Proxies are removed prior to training for the primary sentiment task. The text branch is a TF-IDF Linear Support Vector Machine with a weight of 0.70, and the structured branch is a HistGradientBoosting branch with a weight of 0.30, assigned by validation. On the held-out test set, HTSELM achieves an accuracy of 0.9392, macro-precision of 0.9471, macro-recall of 0.9336, macro-F1 of 0.9398, weighted-F1 of 0.9392, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.9043, Cohen’s kappa of 0.9040, macro ROC-AUC of 0.9923, and macro PR-AUC of 0.9862. The Mean macro-F1 score for Exact 5-fold cross-validation is 0.9398 with an SD of 0.0069. Ablation shows that the dominant signal is text, and the validation-tuned fusion branch offers a relatively small but stable improvement over the text-only branch. There is minimal degradation due to numeric noise, but missing features and text corruption result in gradual degradation. A prospective engagement experiment (excluding engagement-rate components and post-response variables) is similarly close to chance, and the released pre-response variables are not reliable predictors of engagement. The results highlight the importance of leakage auditing, clear feature fusion and careful interpretation when analyzing digital media.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Visual–Inertial Navigation for Autonomous Lunar Surface Mobility: Systems, Datasets, Methods, and Open Challenges
items.abstract: Reliable onboard state estimation plays an important role in autonomous lunar surface mobility, given the lack of conventional global navigation satellite system (GNSS) coverage and the challenges of variable illumination and terrain texture. This review synthesizes model-based, learning-based, and hybrid visual–inertial odometry (VIO) approaches and assesses their relevance to lunar surface operations. The reviewed studies suggest that learned components can improve feature extraction, matching, depth estimation, and measurement confidence in selected datasets and operating conditions. However, representative lunar validation and uncertainty calibration remain limited. Given these limitations, hybrid architectures integrating learned components with explicit model-based estimators offer a comparatively testable design direction. Reduced lunar gravity alone does not render monocular scale unobservable; practical scale–bias performance also depends jointly on motion excitation, inertial quality, visual geometry, calibration, and estimation-window length. Stereo, wheel, crater, and map cues can provide additional metric information but introduce source-specific risks involving calibration, slip, association, and registration. Within the resources surveyed, we found no publicly available flight-derived lunar traverse dataset combining synchronized camera–IMU measurements, independent trajectory ground truth, and onboard timing. Evidence-based priorities include representative lunar validation, uncertainty-aware integration of learned components, consistency monitoring across metric sources, explicit estimator health and fallback mechanisms, and target-hardware resource evaluation.

items.title: Artificial Superintelligence: Must It Be Everywhere? From the Myth of Talos to Infrastructure Dependencies, Operational Authority, and Human Control
items.abstract: Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) raises important questions about the future of artificial intelligence, its potential benefits, and the possibility of losing human control. While many discussions focus on how powerful ASI could become, less attention is given to where it should be used, what authority it should have, and how its dependence on physical infrastructure may create additional risks. Using Talos, the bronze guardian of Greek mythology, as a metaphor for power and physical dependency, this article examines the differences between Artificial Intelligence (AI), Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), and ASI. The study discusses their capabilities, shared infrastructure requirements, and the motivations behind the development of superintelligence. It also distinguishes risks already observed in current AI research from hypothetical scenarios involving future ASI systems. Specific attention is given to energy and critical infrastructure. The article explores the risks that may arise when an intelligent system is granted control over the infrastructure on which its own operation depends. It emphasizes that intelligence, autonomy, and operational authority are different concepts, and that greater intelligence does not necessarily require greater authority. The article proposes a selective, risk-based approach to ASI deployment, supported by limited access permissions, independent safety mechanisms, infrastructure resilience, and meaningful human oversight. Rather than assuming that superintelligence should be integrated into every system, it argues that its use should be determined by actual needs, expected benefits, resource requirements, and the ability to maintain effective human control.

items.title: Asesmen Pembelajaran SD Melalui Artificial Intelligence Berbantuan Zep Quiz Berbasis Adventure Game-Based Learning
items.abstract: Teachers’ limited capacity to develop engaging and adaptive digital assessments, coupled with the underutilization of artificial intelligence (AI), provided the basis for this community service program. The program aimed to improve teachers’ understanding and digital literacy in developing AI-assisted learning assessments using Zep Quiz within an adventure game-based learning approach. It was implemented at SDN 5 Mojolangu with teachers from the elementary school and Islamic elementary school teachers’ working group (KKG) in Lowokwaru District. The program comprised five stages: socialization, training, technology implementation, mentoring and evaluation, and sustainability planning. Its outcomes were evaluated using attendance records, questionnaires measuring understanding, perceived improvement in digital literacy, and program meaningfulness, as well as the products submitted by participants. The program involved 20 teachers, exceeding the initial target of 15 participants. The evaluation results showed a mean understanding score of 3.85 on a four-point scale, categorized as very high; a mean perceived digital literacy improvement score of 3.80, categorized as a substantial improvement; and a mean program meaningfulness score of 4.00, categorized as highly meaningful. All participants successfully developed and submitted 20 Zep Quiz products. These findings indicate that practice-oriented training and mentoring can help teachers integrate pedagogical considerations with technological skills in assessment development. Program sustainability will be supported through classroom trials, peer reviews within the KKG forum, and periodic evaluations to promote the independent and continuous use of digital assessment.
